---
title: "Power series and convergence"
---

## Power series

Power series are special series, which take the form
$$
\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n x^n,
$$
where $\{a_n\}_{n=0}^\infty$ is a sequence and $x\in\mathbb{R}$. We may wonder for what $x$ values such series converge, or not.

As an example, consider the power series
$$
\sum_{n=0}^\infty b_n := \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{x^n}{n!},
$$
where we took $a_n=\frac{1}{n!}$. A natural question here is for what $x$ this sum makes sense. If we use the ratio criterion we get:
$$
\left|\frac{b_{n+1}}{b_n}\right|
=\left|\frac{\frac{x^{n+1}}{(n+1)!}}{\frac{x^n}{n!}}\right|
=\left|\frac{x}{n+1}\right|
\rightarrow 0, \quad \text{as } n\rightarrow \infty.
$$
So we see that we have convergence for all $x\in\mathbb{R}$. In particular this means that the above power series as an infinite sum is always well-defined. So in this way we may define a function $f:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ by
$$
f(x)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{1}{n!}x^n.
$$
Later we will see that this is the well-known exponential function $f(x)=e^x$.

### Convergence intervals

We will show that any power series $\displaystyle\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n x^n$ converges on a symmetric interval around $0$.

::: {#thm-convint} 
**(convergence interval)**
Consider a power series $\displaystyle\sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n x^n$. Then

(i) If $\displaystyle\sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n x^n$ converges when $x=b$, then it converges when $|x|<|b|$.

(ii) If $\displaystyle\sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n x^n$ diverges when $x=b$, then it diverges when $|x|>|b|$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Proof"}

**Case (i).** Suppose that $\displaystyle\sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n b^n$ converges and $b\neq 0$. Then in particular
$$
\lim_{n\rightarrow \infty} c_n b^n=0.
$$
So for $\varepsilon=1$ there is a positive integer $N$ such that
$$
n\geq N \Rightarrow |c_n b^n|<1.
$$
Thus for $n\geq N$ we have
$$
|c_n x^n|
=\left|\frac{c_n b^n x^n}{b^n}\right|
=|c_n b^n|\left|\frac{x}{b}\right|^n
<\left|\frac{x}{b}\right|^n.
$$
If $|x|<|b|$, then $|x/b|<1$ so that $\displaystyle\sum_{n=0}^\infty |x/b|^n$ is a convergent geometric series. Then $\displaystyle \sum_{n=N}^\infty |c_n x^n|$ is also convergent. Hence the series $\displaystyle\sum_{n=0}^\infty |c_n x^n|$ is convergent (absolutely), and therefore $\displaystyle\sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n x^n$ is convergent.

**Case (ii).** Suppose that $\displaystyle\sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n d^n$ diverges. If $x$ is any number with $|x|>|d|$, then $\displaystyle\sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n x^n$ cannot converge, because—by Case (i)—it would imply that $\displaystyle\sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n d^n$ converges.
:::

This theorem shows that either there is a maximal $R\in\mathbb{R}_+$ with convergence on $I=(-R,R)$, or the interval of convergence is all of $\mathbb{R}$.

We cannot say so much about the end-points of those intervals; these have to be checked separately. The theory easily extends to cases where the power series *center* around a value $a\in \mathbb{R}$ instead of $0$, i.e.
$$
\sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n (x-a)^n
$$
for a sequence $\{c_n\}_{n=0}^\infty$. We have the following.

::: {#thm-convint2}
**(convergence interval)**
For a given power series $\displaystyle\sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n(x-a)^n$, there are only three possibilities:

(i) The series converges only if $x=a$.

(ii) The series converges for all $x$.

(iii) There is a positive number $R$ such that the series converges if $|x-a|<R$ and diverges if $|x-a|>R$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Proof"}
First look at power series centered around $a=0$: $\displaystyle\sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n x^n$.

Now suppose that for this series (i) and (ii) do not hold. Then there are nonzero numbers $b$ and $d$ such that $\displaystyle\sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n b^n$ converges and $\displaystyle\sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n d^n$ diverges. Therefore the set
$$
S=\left\{x:\sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n x^n \text{ converges }\right\}
$$
is nonempty. We also know that the series diverges for any $x$ with $|x|>|d|$, so $S$ has an upper bound. Then $S$, being nonempty and bounded, has a least upper bound $R:=\sup S$.

If $|x|>R$, then $x\notin S$, so $\sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n x^n$ diverges. If $|x|<R$, then $|x|$ is not an upper bound for $S$, and so there is $b\in S$ with $b>|x|$. Since $b\in S$, $\displaystyle\sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n b^n$ converges, so must $\displaystyle\sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n x^n$.

Now consider the general case, with $a\neq 0$. Make the change of variable $u=x-a$. Then the power series becomes $\sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n u^n$ and we can apply the former argument to this series. In particular, in case (iii) we have convergence for $|u|<R$ and divergence for $|u|>R$. Thus we have convergence for $|x-a|<R$ and divergence for $|x-a|>R$.
:::

The number $R$ in Theorem @thm-convint2 is called the *radius of convergence* of the power series. We can also summarize the three discussed cases by $R=0$, $R>0$, and $R=\infty$. If $R=0$, the series converges only at a single point, whereas if $R=\infty$ convergence is established for all $x$.





## Examples

::: {.callout-note title="Example: the exponential power series"}
Consider the power series for the exponential function
$$
\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^k}{k!},
$$
and define $a_k=\frac{x^k}{k!}$. Then
$$
\left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right|
=
\left|\frac{\frac{x^{n+1}}{(n+1)!}}{\frac{x^n}{n!}}\right|
=
\frac{|x|}{n+1}
\to 0<1.
$$
So this series converges for **all** $x\in\mathbb{R}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example: $f(x)=\\sum_{k=1}^\\infty \\frac{x^k}{k}$"}
Define
$$
f(x)=\sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac{x^k}{k}.
$$
What is $\mathrm{dom}(f)$?

Use the ratio test with $a_n=\frac{x^n}{n}$. Then
$$
\left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right|
=
\left|\frac{\frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}}{\frac{x^n}{n}}\right|
=
\frac{n}{n+1}|x|
\to |x|.
$$
So the series converges at least for $|x|<1$, i.e. on $(-1,1)$.  
You can also check that it converges for $x=-1$, but not elsewhere. (Does this function look familiar?)
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example: binomial functions"}
The idea of binomials can be extended as follows. For $m\in\mathbb{R}$ and $k\in\mathbb{N}$ define
$$
\binom{m}{k}:=\frac{m(m-1)\cdots(m-k+1)}{k!}.
$$
This agrees with the usual definition when $m,k\in\mathbb{N}$ and $k\le m$:
$$
\binom{m}{k}=\frac{m!}{k!(m-k)!}.
$$

Consider $f(x)=(1+x)^m$ with $m\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{N}$. Then the derivatives do not vanish. We compute
$$
f^{(k)}(x)=m(m-1)\cdots(m-k+1)(1+x)^{m-k}.
$$
The Taylor polynomial at $a=0$ is
$$
T_n(x)
=
\sum_{k=0}^n\frac{f^{(k)}(0)}{k!}x^k
=
\sum_{k=0}^n \binom{m}{k}x^k.
$$

Now consider the limit (a power series):
$$
g(x)=\lim_{n\to\infty}T_n(x)=\sum_{k=0}^\infty \binom{m}{k}x^k.
$$
What is $\mathrm{dom}(g)$?

Apply the ratio test with $a_n=\binom{m}{n}x^n$:
$$
\left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right|
=
\left|\frac{\binom{m}{n+1}x^{n+1}}{\binom{m}{n}x^n}\right|
=
\left|\frac{m-n}{n+1}x\right|
\to |x|.
$$
So the series converges for $|x|<1$ and diverges for $|x|>1$. For $|x|<1$ one obtains the classic identity
$$
(1+x)^m=\sum_{k=0}^\infty \binom{m}{k}x^k.
$$
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example: $(1+x)^{1/2}$"}
Find the Taylor series of $f(x)=(1+x)^{1/2}$.

Compute the first binomial coefficients:
$$
\binom{1/2}{1}=\frac12,\qquad
\binom{1/2}{2}=\frac{\frac12(\frac12-1)}{2!}=-\frac18,\qquad
\binom{1/2}{3}=\frac{\frac12(\frac12-1)(\frac12-2)}{3!}=\frac1{16}.
$$
Hence
$$
\sqrt{1+x}
=
1+\frac12 x-\frac18 x^2+\frac1{16}x^3-\cdots.
$$
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example: $(1-x)^{1/2}$"}
Find the Taylor series of $f(x)=\sqrt{1-x}$.

*Solution:* substitute $-x$ for $x$ in the previous example:
$$
\sqrt{1-x}
=
1-\frac12 x-\frac18 x^2-\frac1{16}x^3-\cdots.
$$
:::
